function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

What I can do is walk you through the exact commands and files you’d need to create locally, so you can execute them yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re not using SSH keys, replace the URL with the HTTPS clone link (`https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`).

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repository & Generate Artifacts

Below are the steps you’d run locally.  
I’ll provide the content for each file you’ll generate.

### 2.1 Detect Predominant Language

Run:

```bash
# Install the language detection tool (optional)
npm install -g language-detection-tool

# Or use a simple script
node -e "
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

function countLines(file) {
  const data = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
  return data.split('\\n').length;
}

function walk(dir, filelist = []) {
  const files = fs.readdirSync(dir);
  files.forEach(file => {
    const fullPath = path.join(dir, file);
    if (fs.statSync(fullPath).isDirectory()) {
      walk(fullPath, filelist);
    } else {
      filelist.push(fullPath);
    }
  });
  return filelist;
}

const files = walk('.');
const stats = {};

files.forEach(file => {
  const ext = path.extname(file).slice(1);
  if (!stats[ext]) stats[ext] = 0;
  stats[ext] += countLines(file);
});

console.log(JSON.stringify(stats, null, 2));
"
```

> **Result** – A JSON object mapping file extensions to total line counts.  
> For a Node.js repo you’ll likely see `js`, `json`, `md`, etc.

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is lightweight and includes Node.js LTS.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * Exposes port `3000` – adjust if your app uses a different port.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` and inside it a file `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Explanation**  
> * `replicas: 3` – adjust based on load expectations.  
> * `image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` – assumes you’ll push a Docker image with this tag.  
> * `Service` exposes the deployment on port `80` externally, routing to container port `3000`.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows` and inside it a file `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '20'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment step here if you want automatic rollout
      run: echo "Deploy step placeholder"
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses `actions/checkout` to fetch the repo.  
> * Installs Node.js 20 and runs tests (`npm test`).  
> * Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
> * You can extend the workflow to deploy to a cluster if desired.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> **Tip** – If you want to stage everything in the repo, you can use `git add .` instead.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Note** – Make sure you have write access to the repo and that your SSH key or personal access token is configured correctly.

---

### Recap of Files Created

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a Docker image for the Node.js app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service YAML for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow to build & push Docker image |

Once you push these changes, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`, build the Docker image, and push it to the registry. If you’ve set up a Kubernetes cluster and configured `kubectl`, you can apply the manifests with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```
